How to play: Slide the power s and the number of terms n, and see the purple line (all numbers) and the green line (only primes) meet.

Sum over all numbersProduct over primes

Look for the math

Euler found in 1737 that a sum over all whole numbers can be written as a product over only the primes. This is the first link between the primes and the function Riemann later studied.

The identity

For s > 1: 1 + 1/2^s + 1/3^s + … = (1 / (1 − 2^−s)) · (1 / (1 − 3^−s)) · (1 / (1 − 5^−s)) · …. Write each factor as a geometric series 1 + p^−s + p^−2s + … and multiply them out. Each term is one product of prime powers, and by unique factorization every whole number n is such a product exactly once, so each 1/n^s shows up exactly once. The logic test confirmed the finite version (primes up to 7, 13 or 5 against the numbers built only from those primes) and that both lines stay under ζ(s) and rise towards it. The page's values ζ(2) = π²/6, ζ(3) and ζ(4) = π⁴/90 were checked to twelve digits.

Why s = 1 matters

At s = 1 the sum is the harmonic series, which has no limit. The product over primes must grow without limit too, so there are infinitely many primes, and they cannot be too sparse. In fact the product up to n grows like e^γ ln n (Mertens), which the test checked up to a million.

The road to the hypothesis

The identity ties the zeta function to the primes. Riemann extended ζ(s) to complex numbers s, where its zeros control how evenly the primes are spread. The Riemann Hypothesis says those zeros all lie on one line. The next pages show how.

Move s down towards 1 and drag n up. How many terms does the sum need before it settles?
